sr.audit.conversion.0.evidence: Buyers must add a cover and a refill separately; the cart suggests nothing. New visitors have to understand the system before buying it.
sr.audit.conversion.0.recommendation: Create a 'Starter System' bundle (cover + 2 refills, 10% off, one Add-to-cart) and make it the primary CTA on cover pages. Bundle-first merchandising typically lifts first-order AOV immediately and reduces choice paralysis.
sr.audit.conversion.0.title: No bundle covers the natural first purchase
sr.audit.conversion.1.evidence: Primary buttons read 'Add to cart'. No urgency, no ownership language anywhere.
sr.audit.conversion.1.recommendation: Use ownership CTAs on cover pages ('Make it yours' opening a color/size selector) and keep 'Add to cart' as the button inside the configurator — same flow, stronger intent framing.
sr.audit.conversion.1.title: CTA verbs are passive
sr.audit.conversion.2.evidence: Payment provider page shows none of your brand or shipping promise; abandonment risk at the last step.
sr.audit.conversion.2.recommendation: If the provider supports it, enable hosted-page theming; otherwise add trust lines immediately before the redirect (returns, delivery estimate, plastic-free packaging).
sr.audit.conversion.2.title: Checkout exits to a generic payment page
sr.audit.messaging.0.evidence: Homepage H1 reads 'Full-grain leather journal covers' with a sub-line about construction. No mention of who it's for or what changes for them.
sr.audit.messaging.0.recommendation: Test a benefit-led H1 for the same visual: 'The last journal you'll ever buy' with sub-copy 'Full-grain leather covers + €12 refills. Made in the EU, plastic-free.' Keep the craft story one scroll below.
sr.audit.messaging.0.title: Hero explains the object, not the outcome
sr.audit.messaging.1.evidence: The refill economy (your core differentiator) appears only on the cover product page, under 'How it works', below the fold.
sr.audit.messaging.1.recommendation: Surface the refill promise in the hero, the navigation ('The System'), and the cart ('this cover takes €12 refills forever'). Make the system diagram — cover, refill, loop — the centerpiece of the homepage.
sr.audit.messaging.1.title: 'Refillable' is buried one click deep
sr.audit.messaging.2.evidence: Product pages read like a workshop spec sheet; the About page is warm and first-person. The shift makes the shop feel anonymous.
sr.audit.messaging.2.recommendation: Move one paragraph of the founder's voice onto every product page ('Why we made this') — consistent warmth, same facts.
sr.audit.messaging.2.title: Tone is inconsistent between product and story pages
sr.audit.pricingPresentation.0.evidence: €12 per 3-pack is listed alone; buyers can't tell if that's good without comparing to a whole new premium notebook.
sr.audit.pricingPresentation.0.recommend: Anchor it explicitly: 'Refills from €4 each — a new premium notebook costs €22.' Show a tiny 3-year cost comparison table (Fernway vs. buying new notebooks).
sr.audit.pricingPresentation.0.title: Refill price has no anchor
sr.audit.pricingPresentation.1.evidence: €69 A5 vs €89 pocket confuses buyers; nothing explains the difference.
sr.audit.pricingPresentation.1.recommend: One sentence per tier ('the pocket uses a rarer, thicker hide'). Confusion at the configurator is where premium carts die.
sr.audit.pricingPresentation.1.title: Cover pricing tiers unexplained
sr.audit.pricingPresentation.2.evidence: Price is presented as a fact; the craft justification lives on a separate page most never visit.
sr.audit.pricingPresentation.2.recommend: A 15-second workshop video adjacent to the price — cost justification at the point of consideration.
sr.audit.pricingPresentation.2.title: No 'why €89' storytelling

sr.executiveSummary.biggestOpportunity: Launch a 'Refill Club' subscription (auto-delivered refills every 2 months) bundled with a first leather cover — it converts your existing one-time buyers into recurring revenue and matches how the product is designed to be used.
sr.executiveSummary.headline: Fernway has a beloved product and a beautiful site — but it is selling stationery like a commodity instead of a ritual, leaving conversion and repeat revenue on the table.
sr.executiveSummary.topFindings.0: The homepage leads with materials and construction, but never names the buyer ('who is this for?') — visitors must self-qualify, and most won't.
sr.executiveSummary.topFindings.1: There is no bundle or refill subscription anywhere in the purchase flow, although the product is literally designed to be refilled — the single biggest repeat-revenue gap.
sr.executiveSummary.topFindings.2: Product pages answer 'what is it made of' in detail but not 'why is it worth 3x a supermarket notebook' — value framing is implicit, not explicit.
sr.executiveSummary.topFindings.3: The site has strong organic basics (fast pages, clean headings, good metadata) but no content answering the questions journal buyers actually search before buying.
sr.market.definition: The premium and refillable notebook segment of the global stationery market — buyers who pay €20+ per notebook (or €70+ per cover system) and choose on quality, aesthetics and values, not price.
sr.market.potentialAssessment: This is a healthy niche with loyal buyers and rising analog-wellness demand, but it is not a winner-take-all market — scale comes from repeat purchase and gift seasonality, not from volume competition. A team of your size can plausibly 2–3x revenue in 12 months with a refill subscription, gift positioning and disciplined content, without paid ads. The main ceiling is production capacity and seasonality cash-flow, not demand.

sr.market.segments.0.name: Daily journaling professionals (25–45)
sr.market.segments.0.why: Highest willingness to pay for a durable daily companion; they replace refills 4–6 times a year.

sr.market.segments.1.name: Fountain-pen & stationery hobbyists

sr.market.segments.2.howToReach: Q4 gift-guide PR, Google Shopping for 'sustainable gift', a gift landing page with note + shipping promise.
sr.market.segments.2.name: Conscious gift buyers
sr.market.segments.2.why: Premium price is an advantage when gifting; the 'buy once, refill forever' story is emotionally resonant.

sr.market.segments.3.name: Corporate & branded gifts
sr.market.segments.3.why: Leather covers deboss beautifully and orders arrive in multiples; slower sales cycle, needs invoicing.
sr.market.size.basis: Sum of regional premium-stationery estimates from two market research summaries [S1][S2]; the refillable sub-segment is not reported separately, so this is an upper bound for the addressable market — treat as directional.
sr.market.trends.0.implication: Journaling is marketed as mindfulness, not office supply — your copy should sell the ritual, and it partially does already.
sr.market.trends.0.trend: Analog wellbeing rituals keep growing post-2020
sr.market.trends.1.implication: 'Plastic-free, refillable, EU-made' belongs in the hero copy and product titles, not only the about page.
sr.market.trends.1.trend: Sustainability is a purchase criterion for premium buyers
sr.market.trends.2.implication: The refill is your consumable — a subscription is the natural second product and your clearest growth lever.
sr.market.trends.2.trend: DTC brands win with subscription consumables
sr.market.trends.3.implication: A dedicated gift flow (gift card, gift note, deadline-guaranteed shipping) can lift Q4 revenue substantially.
sr.market.trends.3.trend: Gift-buying spikes in Q4 and on 'graduation' occasions

sr.strategy.positioning.statement: For people who write every day, Fernway is the journal system that gets better with age — one handmade leather cover, inexpensive refills forever — unlike disposable 'premium' notebooks that you throw away each semester.
